summary: This component detects when a user types the famous Konami code (up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, B, A) and triggers a fun animation of a meerkat running across the screen for three seconds. It handles keyboard input carefully to ignore key repeats and modifier keys that could interrupt the sequence, normalizing key values to work across different keyboard layouts.

explanations.19: This creates a Set of arrow key names for quick lookup — we'll use it later to decide which keys need special handling to prevent page scrolling.
explanations.27: Modifier keys like Shift and Alt fire their own keydown events before the actual letter keys they modify, so we need to skip them or they'd break our sequence detection.
explanations.46: Single-character keys (letters) get converted to lowercase so 'B' and 'A' match whether the user types them normally or with Shift held down, but multi-character keys like 'ArrowUp' stay as-is.
explanations.52: We use a ref instead of state to track progress through the code sequence because refs don't cause re-renders and we don't need to update the display based on progress.
explanations.68: When you hold down a key, the OS sends repeated keydown events; we ignore these to prevent someone holding an arrow key from accidentally injecting extra key presses.
explanations.71: In rare cases (old browsers, event composition systems), event.key might be missing entirely, so we bail out rather than crash.
explanations.77: Arrow keys would normally scroll the page, so we call preventDefault() to stop that behavior while the user is typing the code sequence.
explanations.87: If the key doesn't match what we expected, we reset progress to 0 — but if it matches the first key of the code, we stay at progress 1 in case that key starts a new attempt.
